phonemes.desc: Palatal glide [j] plus mid back [o], closing in the velar nasal [ŋ] — the “yong” of 龍, “dragon”.
Labial-velar glide [w], open [a], and final velar nasal [ŋ] — the “wang” of 王, “king”.

pronunciation.approximation: 'YOHNG-wahng' — Both syllables end in velar nasals. The name is the Sino-Korean title for the dragon king, ruler of the seas.

domains.title: Yongwang, the Dragon King
domains.subtitle: sovereign of the seas, storms, and waters
domains.lead: Yongwang — 龍王, “dragon king” — is the sovereign of the Korean seas: master of storms, rain, and the shoals of fish on which coastal villages live. Reached through Buddhist liturgy, shamanic gut ritual, and village folktale alike, he rewards respect with calm water and punishes neglect with empty nets and sudden gale.

cards.name: Dragon King
cards.desc: The royal dragon enthroned in the underwater palace Yeonggung, sovereign of the four seas of the compass.

cards.name: Ruler of Seas
cards.desc: He governs tides, currents, and the creatures of the deep — the shoals are his armies, the turtles his couriers.

cards.name: Rain and Storms
cards.desc: From his palace he releases the rains that fill the paddies and the typhoons that empty the harbours.

cards.name: Fisherfolk Protector
cards.desc: The south-coast villages honour him with the Yongwang-gut, the annual rite that secures safe voyages and abundant catch.

symbols.name: Dragon
symbols.meaning: The serpent perfected — after a thousand years guarding the yeouiju jewel, the imugi ascends as a true dragon.

symbols.name: Waves
symbols.meaning: The visible form of Yongwang’s domain; the sea’s temper is read as the king’s mood.

symbols.name: Pearl (yeouiju)
symbols.meaning: The wish-granting jewel of the underwater palace — the treasure for which a python waits a thousand years.

symbols.name: Turtle
symbols.meaning: A messenger and attendant of the dragon king, ferrying petitions and souls between land and sea.

mythology.lead: Yongwang is the Dragon King of the Korean seas — sovereign of storms, rain, and the shoals of fish on which coastal life depends. Buddhist scripture, shamanic gut ritual, and village folktale each give him a different throne: a guardian of the dharma, a king placated with offerings set afloat, and a grateful serpent who repays a kindness. His mythology is the story of how Korea learned to live beside a beautiful, dangerous sea.

myths.title: The Python and the Wish-Jewel
myths.text: The Samguk Yusa, “Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms” (13th century), tells of a poor but kind-hearted man who gave shelter to a strange traveller caught by night and rain. The stranger revealed himself as an imugi — a python that had waited a thousand years for the yeouiju, the wish-granting jewel that alone can raise a serpent to dragonhood. Entrusting the jewel to his host, the imugi attempted the ascent to heaven; when it slipped, the man caught it and set it upon the serpent’s head, and the imugi became a true dragon and rose into the sky. In gratitude the dragon left a bright band of his own body coiled around the man’s house as a blessing, and the Samguk Yusa says this is why Koreans paint banded, rainbow colours along the eaves of their houses to this day. The tale teaches that the sea’s greatest power answers to ordinary human kindness — and that even a dragon’s fortune once depended on a stranger’s open door.

myths.title: The King Who Became a Dragon
myths.text: The Samguk Sagi and Samguk Yusa record that King Munmu of Silla (r. 661–681), dying, commanded that his body be cremated and the ashes cast into the East Sea. “I will become a dragon,” he said, “and protect this kingdom from the pirates of the east.” His queen and son fulfilled the vow; the ashes were committed to the sea off the coast near Gampo, and his son King Sinmun raised above the shore the temple Gameunsa — “the temple that appeases the sea” — whose pagodas still stand at Gyeongju. The episode makes explicit what coastal religion had long implied: that the Dragon King and the dead king could share one body, and that the sea’s protection was a royal responsibility, paid for in flesh. Korean Buddhists still honour Munmu as the dragon of the East Sea; the tale binds kingship, Buddhism, and the sea into a single sacred geography.

myths.title: The Yongwang-gut of the Fishing Villages
myths.text: In the fishing villages of Korea’s south coast — Chaeseon in Tongyeong, Suyeong in Busan — shamans performed the Yongwang-gut, the rite of the Dragon King, to open the fishing season and beg calm seas. The folklorist Im Seok-jae recorded these rites in the twentieth century, when they were already old: the shaman invokes the dragon kings of the four seas in turn, receives their possessing presence, and sends a paper dragon-boat laden with rice, fruit, cloth, and coins out onto the water, the offering itself sailing to the palace beneath the waves. If the season proves good, the debt is remembered; if storms come, the rite is repeated with greater care. Here mythology is not a story but a contract renewed each year — a working relationship between a fishing people and the sovereign of the deep, maintained with drum, cymbal, and a boat far too small for its cargo of gratitude.

myths.title: The Monk and the Sea God’s Dream
myths.text: The temple of Haedong Yonggung at Busan, founded in 1376 by the Goryeo monk Naong Hyegeun, stands where cliffs meet the open sea — a rare orientation for a Korean monastery, whose temples customarily turn their backs on the water. Its foundation legend, preserved in the temple’s own tradition, tells that Naong dreamed the Dragon King of the East Sea rose from the waves and showed him a stretch of coast where, if a temple were built, prayers would surely be answered; waking, the dream-site proved to be a rugged shore east of the walled city. He built there, and the fishermen came. The tale reflects the late Goryeo world in which Buddhist and shamanic readings of the sea overlapped completely: the same Dragon King who received paper boats from shamans appeared in the dream of a great Seon master. Visitors still descend the temple’s 108 stairs to the seaside shrine of the dragon king — one of the few places where the old sea cult can be visited, not merely read about.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 龍 (yong, "dragon") and 王 (wang, "king"). Read 용왕 in Korean, it denotes the royal dragon sovereign of the waters, a figure shared across East Asian religions.

nameVariations.note: Alternate term for dragon spirit, especially in shamanic contexts.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Yongwang, the Hangul form is 용왕 and the Hanja form is 龍王. Hangul ‘용왕’ and Hanja ‘龍王’; the figure is shared with East Asian dragon-king traditions but has distinct Korean cultic forms. The ASCII form yongwang is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Yongwang is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Yongwang is part of a broader East Asian dragon-king tradition, with close parallels in Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese religion; the Sino-Korean name itself, 龍王, is borrowed directly. In Korea the figure was absorbed into both Buddhism and shamanism: he appears as a deva-like guardian and rain-maker in Buddhist temples, and as a sovereign spirit who must be formally petitioned in gut rituals. The Chinese cult of the Four Dragon Kings and Daoist rain-making liturgy supplied much of his ceremonial vocabulary. Despite these borrowings, the Korean Yongwang has a distinctive local colouring tied to fishing villages, the south coast, and the hazards of the Korea Strait.
lore.culturalLegacy: Yongwang remains a vivid figure in Korean coastal culture, appearing in temple art, village rituals, seafood markets, and popular media. Dragon king imagery decorates boats, restaurants, and festivals, and prayers for safe fishing continue in many communities. Temples by the sea — Haedong Yonggung above all — keep his cult publicly visible, and the figure also influences Korean environmental thought, serving as a symbol of the sea’s power and the need for respectful relations with marine ecosystems. In games and animation, Yongwang often appears as a majestic dragon lord.
lore.extendedMeditation: Yongwang embodies the oldest human bargain with the sea: reverence in exchange for survival. The ocean that feeds Korea can erase it in a night, and the Dragon King gives that double truth a face, a palace, and a name. He is what a fishing people build when they cannot control the water but cannot leave it either — a sovereign to whom gratitude, offerings, and good behaviour can be addressed. In him the natural and the political also fuse: a king of Silla becomes a dragon to guard the coast, because protecting the realm at sea was understood as the same office as protecting it on land. To study Yongwang is to study how religion works at its most practical: not to explain the storm, but to negotiate with it — year after year, in the only coin a dragon accepts, ceremony.

lore.archaeology: The dragon king left few monumental traces, but his cult surfaces across the peninsula’s material culture. Goryeo and Joseon temple paintings place dragon kings and the underwater palace among the assembly of guardian deities, and the seaside temple of Haedong Yonggung (founded 1376 near Busan) preserves its founder Naong’s dream of the East Sea dragon king as a living foundation charter. The coastal shrine communities of the south sea — Chaeseon and Suyeong among them — anchor the Yongwang-gut traditions recorded by the folklorist Im Seok-jae in the twentieth century. Most strikingly literal is the royal evidence: the underwater tomb of King Munmu’s ashes off Gampo and the twin pagodas of Gameunsa (682 CE) at Gyeongju mark the dynasty’s fusion of kingship with the sea-dragon cult.
